summary: Discovery focused on integration paths for Redwood's hosted, dedicated, and private options. Customer prioritized observability hooks, SDK compatibility (LangChain/LlamaIndex), quota controls and gateway/proxy architecture for rate limiting. Basic security posture (SAML, KMS, audit logs) was validated; next steps center on running micro-benchmarks and sharing detailed prompts and infra diagrams.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-27
Start: 15:30 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Sofia (Redwood AE), Marco (Redwood SE), Alex (Olympus CTO), Priya (Lead ML Eng), Tom (Infra), Nina (PM)
Shared artifacts: https://redwood.example.com/olympus/onramp-proposal (deck), https://s3.olympus.internal/olympus-sample-prompts (placeholder)

[00:00] Sofia (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining — quick roll call?
[00:06] Alex (Olympus): Alex here, Priya, Tom and Nina also on my side.
[00:10] Sofia: Great. Marco's gonna walk through integration options and then we'll align on next steps.
[00:18] Marco (Redwood SE): Cool, hi all. Quick agenda: SDK patterns with LangChain/LlamaIndex, gateway/proxy options for rate limiting, observability hooks and then private deployment constraints.
[00:30] Priya: Sounds good. Our immediate question is — we have an internal retrieval pipeline, LangChain currently, lots of LlamaIndex experiments, we want minimal code changes.
[00:40] Marco: Got it. So Redwood SDKs are lightweight, node and python. Example adapter for Lang Chain is really just an llm client shim — in python you'd swap the openai client for redwood.client, call generate or chat. For Llama Index we have an example connector that patches the llm class.
[00:55] Tom: Do you have an official Lang Chain example? We saw community examples that look brittle.
[01:03] Marco: Yes we have a maintained repo — link in the deck — note that some of the function names differ, and transcription note: sometimes it's 'Lang Chain' in sample code, bad spacing in docs. But the shim handles conversation state and streaming.
[01:20] Nina: Is streaming real-time? We need partial tokens in our frontend.
[01:25] Marco: Streaming is supported, SSE and websockets; SDK exposes an iterator. There's also guidance on chunking long responses.
[01:35] Alex: Big question: hosted vs dedicated vs private. For POC we'd like hosted to move fast but worried about data residency and throughput.
[01:44] Sofia: Totally. Hosted is fastest for dev velocity — no infra. Dedicated gives you reserved GPU slots and predictable throughput/latency. Private is the VPC/on-prem option for compliance. What's your primary constraint?
[01:55] Priya: Two things: observability and quota control. We need token-level cost breakdowns tied to routes and ability to set per-team quotas and throttles.
[02:07] Marco: We expose per-route dashboards and token attribution. For quotas, there are rate limits at the API gateway and per-API-key quotas. You can chain a proxy for additional logic or use Redwood's rate-limit policies.
[02:23] Tom: Would we need a proxy to implement a leaky-bucket burst profile?
[02:27] Marco: Not necessarily — Redwood policy supports burst tokens and sliding windows; but many customers put a sidecar or gateway in front to centralize auth and routing, particularly if they already have a global API gateway.
[02:40] Priya: If we do a sidecar, what about latency overhead? We're targeting p50 60ms for short prompts, p95 < 250ms.
[02:49] Marco: Sidecar adds ~5-15ms typically, depends on network hops. If you require <50ms p50 we often recommend colocated routing or direct SDK calls from app servers. For dedicated clusters we can hit those p50 numbers for short contexts.
[03:05] Alex: Ok. On observability — can we get token-level tracing into our Datadog? We want to correlate user request -> embeddings -> model call.
[03:14] Marco: Yes, we support OpenTelemetry hooks. You can send traces to your backend; Redwood will inject trace ids into metadata. Datadog tracing works via OTLP exporter. Also export token-level cost metrics into metrics backend.
[03:30] Priya: Does that include kv-cache metrics? We need hit/miss counts for prefix caching because our prompts reuse context heavily.
[03:38] Marco: KV cache metrics exposed as part of the runtime telemetry — hit/miss, evictions, cache size per model. Note sometimes the export field names vary, transcription artifact: 'K V cache' in older docs.
[03:50] Alex: Security quick check — SAML SSO for console access? KMS for customer keys? Audit logs?
[03:57] Sofia: Yes to all. Hosted can integrate with SAML SSO for user console. For encryption we support customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM) in Private and Dedicated; hosted has envelope encryption but can integrate with bring-your-own-key via some partner routes. Audit logs are available in console and streamable via webhook or SIEM.
[04:20] Tom: Any SOC2 or ISO attestation?
[04:22] Sofia: We provide SOC2 Type II summary and more — I'll attach the security pack.
[04:26] Priya: About model variants — can Redwood fall back to a smaller model to keep latency SLAs during spikes?
[04:34] Marco: Yes, smart routing can failover to cheaper/quantized variants; policies can be time-based or on load. We also offer automated fallback across regions.
[04:44] Alex: We run LangChain pipeline in a serverless fashion; calls originate from Lambda-like functions. Any issues with cold starts or tokenizing?
[04:54] Marco: If you're calling from ephemeral compute, keep an eye on initial model handshake; SDK reuses connections. For KV cache persistence across ephemeral workers, you'd want a centralized cache layer (Redis) or use Redwood prefix caching at the server.
[05:12] Nina: For LlamaIndex connectors — do you maintain version parity? The ecosystem moves fast and we don't want to babysit adapters.
[05:19] Marco: We maintain tested adapters for the major versions and call out breaking changes. For less common forks we provide a shim pattern. We'll prototype with your exact version in the POC.
[05:30] [Speaker 1]: (inaudible) -- sorry that was background.
[05:35] Priya: Ok, can you walk through the proxy vs gateway tradeoff with an example?
[05:40] Marco: Sure. Example A: You run an API gateway (Kong, Ambassador). You put Redwood SDK calls on the backend; gateway performs auth, then backend calls Redwood directly. This is minimal latency. Example B: You run a centralized proxy that intercepts requests and enforces quotas, headers, and does routing to different model tiers — helpful if you want per-tenant throttles without touching app code. The proxy approach centralizes logic but adds operational surface.
[06:10] Tom: We have an existing gateway and prefer centralizing. How does quota sync work? If we throttle at the gateway and Redwood also has quotas, do they align?
[06:20] Marco: You can push quota events to Redwood via API, or use consistent hashing of API keys. In practice customers run soft-limits at gateway and let Redwood enforce hard limits. We'll provide rate-limit key mapping docs.
[06:34] Alex: Any pitfalls on token accounting? We saw variance between openai and some vendor token counters.
[06:42] Marco: Tokenization differences happen; Redwood provides canonical token counters in the SDK and token-level cost attribution to match billing. For migration we suggest running a side-by-side token audit for a week.
[06:55] Priya: About micro-benchmarks — we'd like to test 3 models: small fast model, mid, and a larger llm we already use. Can Redwood spin up dedicated nodes for a short window?
[07:07] Sofia: For evaluation work we can provision short-term dedicated capacity for controlled runs. We'll need expected QPS and duration. Marco will run a micro-benchmark too.
[07:18] Marco: When running the benchmark I'll measure p50/p95/p99, tail jitter, and cost per 1k tokens across models, and include KV cache hit/miss impact.
[07:28] [00:45] Alex: Great. About deployment — private mode: we have strict firewall rules, no outbound to public internet for models. Does Redwood support air-gapped on-prem?
[07:38] Marco: Yes we have an on-prem package that can be installed behind the firewall. It includes a private control plane option. There are tradeoffs: model updates require a secured sync process. We'll run a security assessment if you go this route.
[07:50] Priya: Key management — HSM or KMS? We use AWS KMS.
[07:54] Marco: AWS KMS supported for Private and Dedicated. Hosted supports envelope encryption and a BYOK pathway through a partner integration — I'll include that in the security pack.
[08:05] Tom: Observability hooks — can we get token-level cost in our event store (Kafka)?
[08:11] Marco: Yes, we can stream cost-events to Kafka. Exporters available: OTLP, Prometheus, and Kafka events.
[08:22] [01:00] Nina: For SDKs — language coverage? Go? Rust?
[08:26] Marco: Official SDKs: Python, Node. Community SDKs: Go and minimal Rust client. For high performance we recommend REST + connection pooling or gRPC in our private offering.
[08:39] Alex: We're using Lang Chain's agent pattern — will function calling semantics map cleanly?
[08:45] Marco: Redwood supports function/tool calling; SDK maps it to LangChain's tool interface. Minor glue code sometimes required for schema. We'll prototype that in the demo.
[08:58] Priya: Rate limits — how granular? Per API key, per route, per team?
[09:04] Marco: All three. You can create policies by api-key, route, org, and even model. There's also a global burst budget per tenant.
[09:14] Tom: Can we prewarm cache / model instances on predictable spikes?
[09:18] Marco: Yes — prewarming and keep-alive tokens are available on Dedicated. For hosted we offer a prewarm API for enterprise customers.
[09:28] Alex: Cost controls — can we set hard caps and alerts?
[09:32] Sofia: Yes, quota alerts, emergency cutoff policies, and per-route budgets are supported. We'll show the console configs.
[09:40] Priya: About retraining or model fine-tuning — we do fine-tuning privately; how does Redwood handle fine-tuned model artifacts?
[09:49] Marco: We can host fine-tuned artifacts in private stores; for hosted we have an upload pipeline with encryption-at-rest. We'll need to validate licensing for base models.
[09:59] [01:30] Alex: Any compliance caveats for EU data residency?
[10:04] Sofia: We offer regional hosting in EU and GCP/ AWS regions. Dedicated and Private give you more assurance for strict residency.
[10:12] Tom: CI/CD integration — we want automatic rollouts with canary.
[10:16] Marco: Redwood Console supports canary rollouts and A/B model routing. You can tie rollouts to traffic % and auto-fallback on regression checks.
[10:27] Priya: Would love to see an eval pipeline connecting our prompt set with Redwood's regression alerts.
[10:33] Marco: We have an Optimize feature that ties prompt sets to QA checks and will alert on quality regressions; you can pipe it into your existing eval infra.
[10:44] Sofia: Ok let's recap next steps: Sofia will send security pack + hosted/dedicated worksheet; Marco will run benchmark and prototype LangChain demo; Olympus to supply prompts and infra diagram.
[10:57] Alex: Sounds good. Any blockers?
[11:00] Tom: Need to confirm legal for data processing agreement, but that's standard.
[11:04] Sofia: We'll loop in legal and CSM on the next call.
[11:08] [01:59] Priya: One more technical — does Redwood produce deterministic tokenization for embeddings across runs? We saw discrepancies previously with different tokenizer versions.
[11:18] Marco: We expose tokenizer version in metadata and can pin tokenizer versions in Dedicated/Private. We'll include tokenizer audit steps in the benchmark.
[11:28] Alex: Great, thanks all.
[11:32] Sofia: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up by EOD with the doc links.

(End of recording)
